correctness.rationale: For 0<s<t, the correlation of the standardized Brownian values is sqrt(s/t). Integrating over both triangles gives E[Z²]=2∫₀¹r q_z(r)dr. Subtracting q_z(0) and integrating by parts yields the weight 1−r² on q′, with the endpoint term zero since q is bounded. The Gaussian density identity ∂_r f=∂_x∂_y f gives two equal positive corners minus two equal negative corners and hence the claimed variance formula. Under the two reciprocal changes of variable the derivative is (D−A)/π with h(s)=sqrt(2s−1)/s². The first moment of the variance kernel is integrable, so V′(0)=∫₀¹2r/[π sqrt(1−r²)]dr=2/π. On a>0 the derivative of log(A/D) is the mean of s on the upper support minus its mean on the lower support, strictly positive. The ratio starts below one and diverges by bounding A below on any compact subinterval of (1/2,1) and D above by a constant times exp(−a). This proves the unique maximum. The upper Laplace piece is O(exp(−a)/a), whereas the lower weight is 8 sqrt(2) sqrt(s−1/2) to leading order, giving the stated Gamma(3/2) constant. Boundedness of coverage proportions gives convergence of their first two moments at each fixed z, not a finite-sample maximizer theorem. Independent quadrature after s=(1+x²)/2 gives a*=0.68810970320346721766…, z*=0.82952378097524559013…, V*=0.08135656185520381043…, nominal coverage 0.59319191415401940057… and SD 0.28523071688582877877…. Independent conditional-Gaussian integration agrees at the displayed threshold.
